title: The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm
summary: Describes the MD5 message-digest algorithm, which takes input of any length and produces a 128-bit fingerprint, or message digest, of the input. It was meant for digital signature applications. It is informational, and MD5 is now known to be weak against deliberate collisions.

eli5.summary: MD5 turns any file into a short fingerprint. If the file changes even a little, the fingerprint changes. People used it to check files were not changed.

questions: how long is an md5 hash
subtitle: The 128-bit fingerprint algorithm that turns a message of any length into a short digest.

tldr.problem: Digital signature schemes need a way to shrink a large file into a small, fixed-size value that can be signed securely with a private key.
tldr.mechanism: MD5 pads the message, appends its length, then mixes each 512-bit block into a four-word buffer through four rounds of 16 operations, and outputs a 128-bit digest.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational, not a standard, and it was updated by RFC 6151. Its security statements are conjectures made in 1992.

today: RFC 1321 is Informational, so it does not define an Internet standard, and it has been updated by RFC 6151. Its collision-resistance statements are conjectures made in 1992.

sections.title: What MD5 Does
sections.content:
MD5 takes a message of arbitrary length and produces a 128-bit message digest, also called a fingerprint. The RFC states it as a conjecture that it is computationally infeasible to produce two messages with the same digest, or any message with a given target digest. It is intended for digital signature applications, where a large file must be compressed in a secure manner before being encrypted with a private key under a public-key system such as RSA.

It is designed to be quick on 32-bit machines and needs no large substitution tables, so it can be coded compactly. The RFC also gives MD5 an OSI object identifier and says the parameters in an X.509 AlgorithmIdentifier should have type NULL.
sections.eli5: MD5 squishes anything, from a postcard to a whole library, into a tiny code. A different input should give a different code.

sections.title: Padding, Length and the Starting Buffer
sections.content:
The algorithm works on a b-bit message, where b may be zero and need not be a multiple of eight. Three preparation steps come first.

  • Padding. A single 1 bit is appended, then 0 bits, until the length is congruent to 448 modulo 512. Padding is always done, even if the message is already that length, so between one and 512 bits are added.
  • Length. A 64-bit representation of the original length b is appended as two 32-bit words, low-order word first. If b exceeds 2^64, only the low-order 64 bits are used. The total is now a multiple of 512 bits.
  • Buffer. Four 32-bit registers A, B, C and D are initialized to the hexadecimal values 01234567, 89abcdef, fedcba98 and 76543210, written low-order bytes first.

Words are 32 bits and bytes are eight bits. Bytes are read into words with the low-order byte first.
sections.eli5: First the message is stretched to a standard size with filler, and its original length is stamped on the end. Then four starting numbers are set up in a mixing bowl.

sections.title: The Four Rounds
sections.content:
The padded message is processed in 16-word (512-bit) blocks. Four auxiliary functions, F, G, H and I, each take three 32-bit words and give one. F acts as a bit-wise conditional (if X then Y else Z), and H is the XOR (parity) of its inputs. A 64-element table T is built from the sine function: T[i] is the integer part of 4294967296 times abs(sin(i)), with i in radians.

For each block, the registers are saved, then four rounds of 16 operations each are applied, one round per function. Each operation updates one register using one of the 16 message words, one table entry and a left rotation by a fixed amount. After the fourth round each register is added to its saved value.

The digest is A, B, C, D in that order, starting with the low-order byte of A and ending with the high-order byte of D.
sections.eli5: Each chunk of the message is stirred into the four numbers by four different recipes, 16 stirs per recipe. When all chunks are done, the four numbers glued together are the fingerprint.

sections.title: Security Claims
sections.content:
The Summary conjectures that finding two messages with the same digest takes on the order of 2^64 operations, and finding any message for a given digest takes on the order of 2^128. It says MD5 has been carefully scrutinized, but is relatively new and that further security analysis is justified.

The Security Considerations section says the level of security is considered sufficient for very high security hybrid digital-signature schemes based on MD5 and a public-key cryptosystem. These are the author's 1992 judgments; for later developments see RFC 6151, which updates this memo.
sections.eli5: When it was written, the author believed it would take a huge amount of work to fool MD5, but he also said more checking was a good idea.

sections.title: Differences From MD4
sections.content:
MD5 extends MD4. It was designed because MD4 was felt to be adopted more quickly than the existing critical review justified, and because MD4, designed to be exceptionally fast, is 'at the edge' for risking cryptanalytic attack. MD5 is slightly slower but more conservative.

The listed differences are:

  1. A fourth round was added.
  2. Each step has a unique additive constant.
  3. The round 2 function was changed to make it less symmetric.
  4. Each step adds in the result of the previous step, promoting a faster avalanche effect.
  5. The order in which input words are accessed in rounds 2 and 3 changed.
  6. Shift amounts were approximately optimized, and the shifts differ between rounds.
sections.eli5: MD5 is a more careful, slightly slower cousin of MD4, with an extra stirring round and tweaks to be harder to break.

sections.title: Reference Code and Test Suite
sections.content:
Appendix A contains a reference implementation in C, taken from RSAREF, a cryptographic toolkit for Privacy-Enhanced Mail. It consists of global.h, md5.h and md5c.c, plus a test driver, mddriver.c, that can also compile for MD2 and MD4. The code uses a context with MD5Init, MD5Update and MD5Final functions, so data can be fed in pieces.

The driver's -x option should print a test suite. For example, the digest of the empty string is d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e and the digest of abc is 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72.
sections.eli5: The RFC includes working code and a list of right answers, so you can check that your own version gives the same fingerprints.

items.title: 1. Pad
items.text: Append a 1 bit and 0 bits until the length is 448 modulo 512.

items.title: 2. Append length
items.text: Add the original length as a 64-bit value.

items.title: 3. Initialize
items.text: Set the four-word buffer A, B, C, D.

items.title: 4. Process blocks
items.text: Mix each 16-word block through four rounds.

items.title: 5. Output
items.text: Emit A, B, C, D as the 128-bit digest.

references.text: Rivest, R., "The MD4 Message Digest Algorithm", RFC 1320, April 1992.
